title: Materials
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Materials Worksheets (Ceramics, Polymers, Composites, Alloys)
standard_text: Properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative); Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling.
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on materials: metals, ceramics, polymers and composites, alloys, choosing materials for a job, natural and synthetic materials, and plastics in the environment. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Choose a material by its properties.
key_sub: Ceramics are hard and brittle; polymers are long chains; composites combine materials.
body_html:
How to think about it

Choose a material by its properties.

  • Metals: strong, malleable, conductors. Ceramics: hard, brittle, heat-resistant insulators.
  • Polymers: long chains of monomers; light, flexible, insulating. Composites combine two materials.
  • Alloys are harder than pure metals. Many plastics are not biodegradable, so recycling matters.
Example

Fibreglass: what type?

Glass fibres in a polymer

Answer: a composite

Example

A plug case: which material?

Insulator, can be moulded

Answer: a polymer

Common mistakes

  • Thinking ceramics conduct electricity.
  • Thinking alloys are compounds.
  • Thinking all plastics are the same.

faq.q: What are ceramics, polymers and composites?
faq.a: Ceramics (such as pottery and glass) are hard, brittle insulators. Polymers (plastics) are long-chain molecules. Composites combine two materials, like carbon fibre or reinforced concrete.

faq.q: Why are alloys used instead of pure metals?
faq.a: Mixing in atoms of a different size stops the layers of metal atoms sliding, so alloys are harder and stronger.

faq.q: Why is plastic waste a problem?
faq.a: Most plastics are not biodegradable, so they build up in landfill and the oceans. Recycling and reducing use help.
